The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) constitute an important component of the State's development framework. extracts.text:
a. Adoption of legally valid GIS-based Master, zonal, and land use plans.

To institutionalize and standardize these initiatives across all Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), Planning Authorities (UDA) it is proposed to mandate the preparation, approval, and adoption of GIS-based Master Plans, including Zonal Plans and Land Use Plans. All concerned authorities shall be required to follow standardized spatial and attribute structures, obtain statutory approval from the competent authority, and ensure formal adoption under relevant planning laws.

b. All ULBs/Authorities are directed to upload approved GIS based Plans for public access.

Further, all ULBs and UDAs shall be mandated to upload approved GIS-based plans on their official web portals and ensure public accessibility through user-friendly platforms.

c. Regulatory framework shall be established.

It is also proposed to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework defining the methodology, spatial standards and regulations of master plan preparation encompassing the processes such as baseline study with benchmarks, preparation of base map, preparation of existing land use map, existing situation analysis, identification of gaps and demands, stakeholders engagement, development proposals, preparation of proposed land use map, formulating the draft master plan and notifying final master plan using a standard operating procedure to ensure compliance and accountability.

Spatial Standards are as follows:

e Mapping Scale ~ Master Plan: 1:4,000; Zonal Plan: 1:2,000; Local Area Plan (LAP): 1:1,000; Site Plan: 1:500

e Horizontal Datum: World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS 84)

e Map Projection: Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)

e Vertical Datum: WGS 84 Ellipsoidal Height, converted to Mean Sea Level (MSL) using an appropriate Geoid Model.

d. The spatial database shall include comprehensive GIS layers such as administrative boundaries, cadastral parcels (where available), transportation networks, existing and proposed land use, building footprints, water bodies, drainage, contours and terrain, utilities (water supply, sewerage, storm water, electricity, gas, telecommunications), environmental features, heritage assets, public and community facilities, green and open spaces, disasterprone areas, infrastructure corridors, and demographic and socioeconomic attributes linked through spatial identifiers.

e. The implementation of the above measures will result in a standardized, transparent, and legally robust planning system, enabling efficient urban development and improved governance. It will also strengthen public access to planning information and support data-driven decision-making.

4. In view of the above, the Commissioner of Town and Country Planning has requested the Government to issue necessary orders for mandating the preparation, approval, and adoption of legally valid GISbased Master Plans, Zonal Plans, and Land Use Plans, and directing all ULBs/Authorities to upload the approved GIS-based plans for public access, and for the establishment of a regulatory framework for standardized methodologies and GIS data layers.

hazard restrictions.

It is proposed that formal land use planning and zoning regulations shall mandatorily incorporate critical parameters such as the availability of trunk infrastructure, including water supply, electricity, and sanitation systems, to ensure that development is aligned with service capabilities. Further, hazard mapping shall form an integral component of planning, identifying areas where development is prohibited due to natural hazards. In addition, hazard maps_ shall specify minimum separation between residential zones and hazardous occupancies. Accordingly, it is proposed to mandate the preparation and enforcement of land use plans and zoning regulations incorporating mandatory infrastructure requirements

and hazard-based restrictions.

construction areas

There is a need to establishing a regulatory framework that defines zoning parameters based on the availability and adequacy of trunk infrastructure. 1.Preparation and enforcement of land use planning and zoning regulations incorporating infrastructure and

hazard restrictions.

It is proposed that formal land use planning and zoning regulations shall mandatorily incorporate critical parameters such as the availability of trunk infrastructure, including water supply, electricity, and sanitation systems, to ensure that development is aligned with service capabilities. Further, hazard mapping shall form an integral component of planning, identifying areas where development is prohibited due to natural hazards. In addition, hazard maps_ shall specify minimum separation between residential zones and hazardous occupancies. Accordingly, it is proposed to mandate the preparation and enforcement of land use plans and zoning regulations incorporating mandatory infrastructure requirements

and hazard-based restrictions.

2.Hazard maps shall be formally approved and published with prohibited zones, separation distances, no

construction areas

Further, hazard maps identifying prohibited zones, minimum separation distances, and no-construction areas shall be prepared, duly approved by the competent authority, and published for public access to ensure transparency and

awareness and implementation.

3.Establishing a regulatory framework to define zoning parameters based on availability of trunk infrastructure

There is a need to establishing a regulatory framework that defines zoning parameters based on the availability and adequacy of trunk infrastructure. This framework shall ensure that development permissions are granted only where infrastructure systems are sufficient or planned to meet the projected demand, thereby preventing overburdening of services and ensuring orderly growth.

4. The above proposed measures are expected to result in a scientifically robust and legally enforceable planning system that promotes sustainable development, enhances public safety, protects natural resources, and ensures efficient utilization of infrastructure. It will also improve transparency, strengthen governance, and support informed decision-making.

5. In view of the above, the Commissioner of Town and Country Planning has requested the Government. issue necessary orders mandating the integration of infrastructure availability and hazard considerations into land use planning and zoning regulations, approving -and publishing hazard maps indicating prohibited zones, separation distances, and no-construction areas, and establishing a- regulatory framework to define zoning parameters based on the availability of trunk infrastructure.

6. After careful consideration, the Government hereby, accept the request of Commissioner of Town and Country Planning and issue orders for mandating the integration of infrastructure availability and hazard considerations into land use planning and zoning regulations, approving and publishing hazard maps indicating prohibited zones, separation distances, and. no-construction areas, and establishing a regulatory framework to define zoning parameters based on the availability of trunk infrastructure.

To address the ongoing epidemiological transition, Tamil Nadu has established 708 Urban Health and Wellness Centres (UHWCs) with one UHWC for every 15,000 to 20,000 population for providing 12 Comprehensive Primary healthcare services in close proximity to Urban communities,

54

ensuring accessible primary healthcare and thereby reducing the burden on Secondary and Tertiary healthcare facilities.

All 708 UHWCs are staffed by a dedicated team of a Medical Officer, Staff Nurse, Health Inspector and Support staff. To improve accessibility for the Urban working population, UHWCs function on two shifts, from 8:00 AM to 12:00 Noon and from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM. Since their inception, these centres have provided healthcare services to 4.54 crore Urban beneficiaries, as reported in the U-AAM portal.

c) Urban Polyclinics

Urban Polyclinics have been established to ensure continuity of care by bringing specialist services closer to the community, thereby reducing the need for patients to travel to tertiary hospitals for specialist consultations.

The establishment norm for Urban Polyclinics is to have one polyclinic for every 5-6 UPHCs, covering an approximate population of 2.5 to 3 lakh persons. Polyclinics function during evening hours (4:30 PM to 8:30 PM) to maximise accessibility for the working population.

55

A total of 154 Urban Polyclinics are presently operational across the State, providing specialist outpatient services across nine disciplines namely General Medicine, Paediatrics, Dentistry, Ophthalmology, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Dermatology, Psychiatry, Physiotherapy and Orthopaedics (only at Poonamallee). Totally 5.61 lakh beneficiaries have utilised Polyclinic services during 2025-26 (HMIS 3.0).

d) City Public Health Laboratories

City Public Health Laboratories have been established under the 15th Finance Commission to

56

strengthen diagnostic services at Urban health facilities. CPHLs function as referral diagnostic hubs for UPHCs and UHWCs and contribute significantly in reducing out-of-pocket expenditure by providing diagnostic services free of cost to the Urban population.

A total of 35 CPHLs have been established across the State equipped with advanced diagnostic equipment including Fully Automated Analyzers which run wide range of biochemical investigations.

e) Community Engagement Activities

NFHS-6 demonstrates that social determinants continue to influence health outcomes, including maternal nutrition, child nutrition and health-seeking behaviour. Recognising that healthcare services alone cannot address these challenges, NUHM promotes community participation through observance of Urban Health & Nutrition Day facilitated by Urban Health Nurses and Mahila Arogya Samitis / Pengal Nalavazhvu Kuzhu.

A total of 3,349 Mahila Arogya Samiti (MAS) groups have been established across the

57

11 Municipal Corporations of Tamil Nadu which serve as community platforms for promoting health awareness and improving water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition and for encouraging positive health-seeking behaviours among slum and vulnerable populations.

The Civil Supplies and Consumer Protection

During the period of the second World War,

Over the years, the rationing system was

Through this system, essential commodities such

Tamil Nadu is the only State in India

met without any discrimination based on

ORDER:

The White Paper on fiscal management of Tamil Nadu that was published in June 2026 sets the roadmap for better revenue mobilisation and administrative reforms, and has inter alia observed that the decline across major taxes like GST, VAT, and excise including revenues from mines and minerals has been mainly driven by administrative choices, leakages and corruption in the past rather than an underlying economic slowdown. It has also indicated that resolving this shortfall requires long-term, multi-year reforms focused on curbing corruption, enforcing compliance, and mobilizing resources efficiently. Some of the key factors highlighted in the White Paper are outlined below:

e Own-tax effort at a historic low — the SOTR-to-GSDP ratio fell to 5.45% in 2025-26, the lowest in two decades showing the sharpest decline among peer States in recent years.

5. 1. Agri Marketing

5.1.1. Regulated Markets

Regulated Markets are functioning in

Tamil Nadu to regulate the sale of agricultural

produce and ensure that farmers receive a fair

price without the involvement of intermediaries.

These markets have been established under the

Tamil Nadu Agricultural Produce Marketing

(Regulation) Act, 1987 and the Rules, 1991.

At present, 285 Regulated Markets are functioning

under the control of 27 Market Committees.

Regulated Markets serve as a common

platform where farmers can sell their produce

183

directly. Here, farmers participate in the closed

bidding and obtain better prices for their produce.

At Regulated Markets, farmers receive a fair

price as their produce is accurately weighed and

prices are determined according to quality. No fee

is collected from farmers for this service.

A market fee of 1 percent of the sale value of the

produce is collected from traders.

Pledge loans are provided to farmers up to a

maximum of Rs.5 lakh and to Farmer Producer

Companies up to Rs.10 lakh at an interest rate of

5 percent for a period of up to 6 months (one

year for Turmeric). Traders are provided pledge

loans up to a maximum of Rs.2 lakh at an interest

rate of 9 percent.

During the current year, action is being taken

to regulate the trade of 56 lakh metric tonnes of

agricultural produce through Regulated Markets

Rs.77 crore.

A total of 322 storage godowns with a

capacity of 4.55 lakh metric tonnes in Regulated

Markets have obtained accreditation from the

Warehousing Development and Regulatory

Authority. Farmers and traders can store their

agricultural produce in these storage godowns

produce, against electronic Negotiable Warehouse
